parakeet: Christianity claims that human beings are uniquely made in the image of God. But what does that actually mean? If humans are physical, embodied, carbon-based, evolutionary products who are visibly seen, while God is non-physical, invisible, undetectable, and completely beyond perception, in what meaningful sense are we made in his image? He'll tell you the image doesn't mean physical appearance, it means human rationality, our morality, our creativity, our capacity for deep relationship or our spiritual likeness. But notice the absolute failure of local biology here. Every single one of those traits, our morality, capacity to love, creative drives, our logical reasoning is explicitly undeniably tied to our physical brains. If you alter the physical brain with an injury, you alter the person's morality. If you flood the brain with chemicals, you alter their capacity for logic and relationship. Our highest attributes are not floating in a non-physical ether. They are the direct output of complex physical biological systems. So if God has no brain, no body, no biological history, and no physical presence, the phrase the image of God is doing zero cognitive work. It has no actual correspondence to reality. It's functioning purely as a poetic security blanket. You don't get to use the image of God when it helps elevate human significance, then retreat to God is beyond perception when asked about what that image actually corresponds to. When confronted with a universe where God is uniquely unobservable, the most common theological escape hatch is simple. God wants faith rather than certainty. But how can a preference be affirmed before the entity has been confirmed? Before anyone can confidently tell you that God wants faith, they're structurally obligated to establish four massive foundational premises. God exists, God has personal desires and psychological motives. Those cosmic desires can be reliably known by human beings, and their specific religious tradition is the one accurately reporting them. Without verifying those four pillars first, the phrase God wants faith isn't an explanation. It's a theological assumption masquerading association. The believer is saying God remains hidden because God wants faith, but they only know God wants faith if they already assume God exists and that their tradition accurately communicates God's intention. So the argument becomes God is hidden because God wants faith, and we know God wants faith because of the religious framework that already assumes God. That's not an explanation. That's internal reasoning inside the belief system. God wants faith does not solve the problem of divine hiddenness. It depends on divine hiddenness already being explained away by the belief system. Before you can explain to me why a creator chooses to remain unconfirmed, you first have to show me that there is a creator out there to have a preference in the first place, and that you somehow have access to its psychological profile.
